beats.care: Satellite internet could bring fast data to villages and hills with no towers. More players could also mean cheaper plans for you.
beats.what: Elon Musk posted on X calling Mukesh Ambani India's real boss, because his Starlink internet service still can't launch here.
beats.why: Starlink has a licence but still needs a security clearance. The government says Jio's and OneWeb's satellite services are at the same stage.

cards.body: Musk first said unnamed 'oligarchs' were blocking Starlink. The telecom ministry called claims of unfair treatment 'baseless and misconceived', saying security checks are mandatory for every satellite licensee. Hours later, Musk posted 'Dear Prime Minister Ambani'. Akash Ambani said he hadn't seen the remarks.

a.body: Starlink has spent five years following Indian rules and is licensed in over 165 countries. He claims a telecom monopoly wants to keep it out.
a.label: Elon Musk says

b.body: All three licensed satellite firms, including Jio's, are at the same stage. The security check is pending with the Home Ministry and isn't about one company.
b.label: Government says

cards.body: Instead of cables and towers, a small dish talks to satellites overhead. That makes it handy for remote villages, ships and disaster zones, though it usually costs more than mobile data. After security clearance, firms still need spectrum assigned before they can sell plans.
cards.title: how is satellite internet different?

cards.body: Starlink says it has already built 20 gateway sites in India, with hundreds of antennas, while it waits for the green light.
